summary: The article argues that youth aged 18 to 29 are vital to local governance and examines barriers to their voting in municipal elections, including low political education, confusing registration, inconvenient voting hours, mobility and the digital divide. It proposes strategies such as civic education in schools, personal contact campaigning and modernized voting, and cites success stories from Leyton and Thomasville. It closes with calls ahead of the October 14, 2023 elections to simplify registration, improve digital accessibility and include youth voices in policymaking.
one_line: Article on barriers keeping young voters from municipal elections and strategies, including civic education, extended hours and ambassador programs, to boost youth turnout.
key_facts: The municipal elections take place on October 14, 2023, and the article defines youth as individuals aged 18 to 29.

Dr. Emily Robertson, a political science lecturer at University City College, says there is a substantial gap in youth knowledge of local governance because national politics dominates media and school discussions.
Jake Muller, a 22-year-old college student, could not vote in the last council election because the online registration process was unclear and his application was never confirmed.
Standard weekday voting hours conflict with young adults' school and work schedules.
Young people often move for education or work, which distances them from home-town elections and weakens the sense of community that strongly predicts local electoral participation.
The digital divide means some youth lack resources or digital literacy, and candidates focused on social media and online platforms alienate them.
Sarah Benson, a community organizer in Millbrook, notes that a sizeable minority without regular internet access miss crucial campaign information.
Proposed strategies include political education in school curriculums, door-to-door campaigning and community events at schools, colleges and youth hangouts, and online or app-based voting.
Tech analyst and political blogger Martin Greene suggests app-based voting, saying this generation 'does everything on their phones – shops, banks, dates. Why not vote?'
Leyton ran a 'youth vote ambassador' program in which young locals educated peers about voting and registration; ambassador Alexandra Hughes, 19, reported a noticeable uptick in young voter turnout.
Thomasville's board of elections extended polling hours and added weekend voting; resident Madeline Choi said this let many people vote without sacrificing work or study time.
Dr. Naomi Peterson, a local governance researcher, says youth voices must be included in policymaking and campaigning because today's policies will long affect the younger generation.
